Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21

Exercises for Chapter 21 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: Italian, French, German and enharmonic German sixth chords, writing them, naming them, lead-sheet symbols, telling them from V7/N by spelling and from iv6 and N6 by ear, the descending chromatic bass line, and the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 21, Augmented Sixth Chords of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows the other chromatic chords: secondary dominants (Chapter 17) and secondary diminished chords (Chapter 18).

Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then where it goes: to V, or (German sixths) to I64 and then V.

Typing: notes with spaces, bass first (Ab C Eb F#). Chord symbols as Ab7, Ab7(b5), Ab7(no5). The chords’ names as It, Fr, Ger, EnGer (with or without +6).

21.1 Augmented sixth chords

An augmented sixth chord leads to the dominant from both sides at once. ♭6 in the bass falls a half step to 5, and ♯4 above it rises a half step to 5. The two notes are an augmented sixth apart, so they move outward to an octave. In C, that’s A♭ and F♯ moving to the two Gs. In a minor key, ♭6 is already in the key signature, so only ♯4 needs an accidental. These chords do a pre-dominant’s job: they come before V. Read 21.1

21.2 The three types

All three start from the same three notes: ♭6, 1 and ♯4. What’s added decides the name:

Chord Notes (scale degrees) In C In c minor
Italian, It+6 ♭6 1 ♯4 (1 is doubled in four parts) A♭ C F♯ A♭ C F♯
French, Fr+6 ♭6 1 2 ♯4 A♭ C D F♯ A♭ C D F♯
German, Ger+6 ♭6 1 ♭3 ♯4 A♭ C E♭ F♯ A♭ C E♭ F♯
Enharmonic German, EnGer+6 ♭6 1 ♯2 ♯4 A♭ C D♯ F♯ (major only)

The EnGer+6 sounds the same as the German sixth, but ♭3 is spelled ♯2, because it rises to 3 of a major I64. It only occurs in major keys. The book notes that the national names have no known reason behind them. Read 21.2

21.3 Analysing augmented sixth chords

Stack any of these chords in thirds and you find a diminished third (A♭ C E♭ F♯ in C becomes F♯ A♭ C E♭, where F♯ to A♭ is a diminished 3rd). No chord met before this chapter has one, so the book’s rule is: a diminished third means an augmented sixth chord. Then find ♭6 and ♯4, and the remaining note tells you the type. Read 21.3

21.4 Lead-sheet symbols

A chord symbol shows root, quality and inversion, not where notes go, and there is no chord symbol with a diminished third. So for lead-sheet symbols, the book treats each augmented sixth chord as a dominant seventh on ♭6 whose seventh is misspelled (F♯ for G♭):

  • It+6 → A♭7 (no 5th)
  • Fr+6 → A♭7(♭5)
  • Ger+6 and EnGer+6 → A♭7

That’s how the chords are written in jazz and pop, and it matches how they sound. Read 21.4

21.5 Examples

The book’s examples, cut where the book cuts them. The popular-music ones (Ellington, Coltrane, Mancini, Fiona Apple, Menken) spell the chord as a 7th chord on ♭6, as in 21.4. “Friend Like Me” repeats Am – F7 – E: i – Ger+6 – V. Read 21.5

21.6 Telling chromatic chords apart

What to look for first, after the book’s Table 21.6.1:

Chord Look for Labels
Secondary dominant its quality: major triad or 7th chord V/x, V7/x
Secondary diminished its quality: °, ø7 or °7 vii°/x, viiø7/x, vii°7/x
Mode mixture lowered notes (borrowed from minor) iv, ii°, iiø7, ♭VI, …
Neapolitan a major chord on ♭2 N
Augmented sixth a diminished 3rd when stacked in thirds It+6, Fr+6, Ger+6, EnGer+6

Read 21.6

The German sixth and a dominant 7th on ♭6 sound the same. Only the spelling tells them apart: - A♭ C E♭ F♯ in C is a Ger+6, going to V. - A♭ C E♭ G♭ is a dominant 7th, V7 of D♭. D♭ is the Neapolitan in C, so the chord is V7/N. (Naming it V7/N is this site’s addition; the book’s chapter on the Neapolitan is Chapter 20.)

21.7 Descending chromatic bass lines

A bass line that falls by half steps from 1 to 5 (1 – 7 – ♭7 – 6 – ♭6 – 5) turns up in music of every century since the 1600s, under many different chords. The book’s table lists how each of its examples harmonizes it. Read 21.7

Here is the harmonization the book lists for Beethoven’s 32 Variations in C minor (i – V6 – V42/iv – IV6 – Ger+6 – i64), here with a V – i added to finish. The voicing is this site’s, not Beethoven’s:

21.8 Chromatic pre-dominant chords

The chapters on chromatic chords add new members to the pre-dominant group. Besides IV and ii there are now V/V and vii°/V, the borrowed iv and iiø7, the Neapolitan N6, and the three augmented sixths. Read 21.8

Five of them have ♭6 or 4 in the bass, so they are easy to confuse by ear. This drill plays I – ? – I64 – V – I and asks for the second chord. Things to listen for: - iv6 and N6 are plain triads. - It+6 is thin: only three different notes. - Ger+6 sounds like a dominant 7th. - Fr+6 has its own colour: all four of its notes belong to one whole-tone scale.

Keys: v, n, i, f, g.

NoteFor teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • Chords drilled: the book’s Figure 21.2.1. It+6, Fr+6 and Ger+6 in major and minor; EnGer+6 in major only. Lead-sheet symbols as in Figure 21.4.1. The It+6 is shown and asked for with three notes; a written answer with the doubled tonic is accepted.
  • V7/N (A♭ C E♭ G♭ in C) is the site’s addition, for 21.6. It’s off except in the 21.6 drill and the last one.
  • Resolution: ▶ Hear it plays It+6 and Fr+6 to V, Ger+6 and EnGer+6 to I64 then V, and V7/N to N6. The voicings are close position above the bass: the drills are for spelling and labelling, not voice leading.
  • The ear drill voices every chord in four parts in C and moves it to the key. In minor, the tonic chords are minor. The frame (I – ? – I64 – V – I) is the same for every answer, so the length gives nothing away.
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/aug6-drill.test.js generates over 10,000 questions and checks each one by its own arithmetic: the scale degrees of every note, the augmented 6th, what is drawn against what is played, and which typed answers are accepted or refused.
